paragraphs: Distributed training can become expensive when workers must repeatedly exchange information with a central server. This paper studies convex optimization when communication is costly in both directions. Its method, 2Direction, combines compressed messages with acceleration, aiming to reduce the communication needed to solve the optimization problem.

The central technical ingredient is a new error-feedback mechanism for handling compression errors. The authors find that two existing mechanisms, EF and EF21-P, which have worked well for non-accelerated methods, are unsuitable for accelerated methods. Their replacement is designed specifically to make bidirectional compression compatible with acceleration.

For strongly convex problems, the paper proves improved communication complexity, replacing some previous dependencies with square-root expressions while accounting for compression quality, smoothness, and worker count. It also reports improvements for general convex problems and identifies 2Direction as the first method to improve on vanilla accelerated gradient descent's communication complexity. Experiments support the theoretical results. The contribution concerns communication efficiency within these optimization settings, with a mechanism tailored to that objective.
neurips-2023-2direction-theoretically-fa.tldr: 2Direction combines acceleration, bidirectional compression, and a new error-feedback mechanism to improve communication complexity in distributed convex optimization.

paragraphs: Answering a question from complete information differs from investigating a situation where important evidence is missing. This paper introduces Conan, an interactive open-world environment for evaluating that second ability. Agents must explore their surroundings, gather information, and combine new observations with existing knowledge to explain events.

The environment emphasizes multiple rounds of abductive reasoning: working from incomplete observations toward an explanation of what happened. This makes information gathering part of the reasoning task itself. An agent cannot rely solely on a single instruction-following deduction from facts already supplied; its interactions help determine which evidence becomes available for subsequent reasoning.

The authors' analysis finds shortcomings in contemporary leading models' active exploration and understanding of complex situations. They also investigate Abduction from Deduction, an approach that uses Bayesian rules to reformulate abductive inference as a deductive process. Conan's main contribution is an environment for studying these abilities together, making it possible to assess reasoning that depends on continued engagement with the world.
neurips-2023-active-reasoning-in-an-open.tldr: Conan evaluates whether agents can actively gather evidence and reason through incomplete-information situations in an interactive world.

paragraphs: A directed cyclic graph represents directed relationships that can form feedback loops. Constructing such a network is computationally and algorithmically challenging, and comparing several networks adds the problem of identifying how causal relationships differ. This paper addresses network construction and comparison through a shared structural model.

The proposed method uses limited information to construct multiple networks simultaneously and infer their disparities. Treating the networks within one model brings estimation and comparison into the same procedure. The resulting differences can be visualized using correspondence analysis, connecting the statistical comparison to a representation that helps expose relationships across networks.

The algorithm has two sequential stages, each containing tasks that can run in parallel as network complexity grows. With high-performance clusters, this organization makes bootstrap evaluation of statistical significance feasible. The authors also establish non-asymptotic theoretical properties, meaning their analysis is not restricted to an infinite-data limit. Applications to synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness for jointly learning and comparing these networks.
neurips-2023-analysis-of-variance-of-mul.tldr: A shared structural model enables joint estimation, statistical comparison, and visualization of multiple directed cyclic causal networks.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning and self-training both make use of unlabeled data, but their usefulness together is a separate question from their individual success. This paper systematically studies their combination in two settings: domain adaptation, where the data distribution changes, and semi-supervised learning without that distribution shift.

The experiments reveal an important distinction. Under distribution shift, the two techniques provide substantial complementary benefits. Across eight distribution-shift datasets, their combination achieves accuracy reported as 3–8% higher than either method alone. In the semi-supervised setting without shift, however, the authors do not find synergistic benefits. The practical value of combining them therefore differs across the investigated settings.

A theoretical analysis offers an explanation within a simplified model of distribution shift. It identifies scenarios where contrastive learning produces features that give self-training a useful starting point. Self-training can then strengthen those gains and reach optimal performance, even when either technique alone would fail. This is a conditional account of how the methods can cooperate, supporting the empirical finding without asserting that their combination always helps.
neurips-2023-complementary-benefits-of-c.tldr: Contrastive learning and self-training provide complementary gains under distribution shift, but the same synergy was not observed without shift.

paragraphs: Text-to-3D methods guided by 2D diffusion models can produce objects whose appearance becomes inconsistent when viewed from different directions. A striking example is the Janus problem, where a canonical feature such as a face appears on other sides of the object. This paper identifies biases embedded in the 2D models as main causes of these inconsistencies.

The authors propose two interventions within score-distillation frameworks. Score debiasing truncates the scores supplied by the diffusion model, gradually raising the truncation threshold during optimization. Prompt debiasing uses a language model to identify conflicts between the user's description and view-specific prompts, while adjusting discrepancies between those prompts and the object's viewing direction.

These interventions address both the model's numerical guidance and the language used to specify views. Experiments show substantially fewer artifacts and more realistic generated objects, with little overhead. The reported outcome is a favorable balance between following the 2D diffusion model and maintaining 3D consistency. The methods reduce the view-consistency problem rather than establishing that every generated object is free of it.
neurips-2023-debiasing-scores-and-prompt.tldr: Debiasing diffusion scores and view prompts reduces inconsistent appearances and artifacts in text-to-3D generation with little overhead.

paragraphs: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning is difficult when an agent receives a reward only after reaching its goal. Adding intermediate rewards can help, but misaligned rewards can encourage suboptimal behavior, and their effectiveness can depend on the learning algorithm. This paper proposes f-Policy Gradients, or f-PG, as a framework for supplying denser exploration signals.

The method minimizes an f-divergence between the agent's state-visitation distribution and the goal. This shifts attention toward where the policy takes the agent over time. The authors derive policy gradients for several divergences and show that optimizing this type of objective can lead to an optimal policy.

The framework also includes an entropy-regularized special case called state-MaxEnt RL. Several distance-based shaping rewards, including L2, can be used within this formulation, providing a common setting for studying reward shaping alongside exploration. Experiments report better performance than standard policy-gradient methods on a challenging gridworld, Point Maze, and FetchReach. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support distribution-based objectives as a useful approach to sparse-reward learning.
neurips-2023-f-policy-gradients-a-genera.tldr: f-PG uses divergences between state visitation and goals to provide dense exploration signals and can lead to optimal goal-conditioned policies.

paragraphs: A stochastic bandit algorithm repeatedly chooses among options with uncertain rewards, trying to limit the reward lost through imperfect choices. This paper studies that regret-minimization problem without imposing a parametric reward model. Its setting assumes that rewards have a known upper bound, under which asymptotically optimal algorithms already exist.

The obstacle is their practical cost. Existing optimal methods depend on an infimum of Kullback–Leibler divergences, a distribution-comparison quantity that is expensive to compute. They also require storing all previous rewards. Consequently, simpler algorithms are often used even though they lack the same optimality guarantees.

The authors introduce several approximations to this KL-based quantity that substantially reduce computation and memory requirements while preserving the regret guarantees. They use the results to construct new versions of MED and IMED and examine them through extensive numerical simulations. The significance is that cheaper computation need not require giving up the established long-run regret guarantees in this setting. The stated optimality remains asymptotic and tied to the assumed reward bound.
neurips-2023-fast-asymptotically-optimal.tldr: New KL approximations reduce the computation and memory costs of non-parametric bandit algorithms while preserving their asymptotic regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Image-goal navigation asks an agent to reach a location specified by a picture taken there. The agent must connect details in that target picture with its current observations. Existing methods often encode the goal and observation separately, combining their features only when predicting navigation actions.

FGPrompt addresses two weaknesses of that arrangement: losing detailed goal information and interpreting the current view without knowing which regions matter for the goal. It uses high-resolution, fine-grained feature maps from the goal image as prompts that condition observation encoding. Goal information therefore influences how the current scene is represented, preserving details and directing attention toward relevant regions.

The authors report significant improvements on Gibson, MP3D, and HM3D. On Gibson, they report an 8% improvement over the state-of-the-art success rate while using a model one-fiftieth the size. These results support the value of introducing detailed goal information into observation processing itself. In the evaluated settings, this design improves navigation performance while also enabling a much smaller model.
neurips-2023-fgprompt-fine-grained-goal-.tldr: FGPrompt conditions visual observation encoding on detailed goal-image features, improving image-goal navigation with a substantially smaller model on Gibson.

paragraphs: This paper studies how accurately a particular autoencoder can remove noise from data drawn from a Gaussian mixture. The architecture has two nonlinear layers, tied weights, and a skip connection. Rather than evaluating the architecture only through experiments, the authors derive mathematical expressions for its denoising performance.

The analysis uses a specific high-dimensional regime: the input dimension and number of training examples both grow without bound, while the number of hidden units remains bounded. Within that setting, the authors obtain closed-form expressions for mean-squared test error. These expressions make the model's prediction error quantitatively accessible under the stated data and architecture assumptions.

The results also quantify the advantage of including the skip connection over an autoencoder without it, which is closely related to principal component analysis. This gives a direct architectural comparison through denoising error. The authors further show that their theory accurately captures learning curves on a range of real datasets, indicating that the analysis can describe observed behavior beyond the Gaussian-mixture setting used for the derivation.
neurips-2023-high-dimensional-asymptotic.tldr: A high-dimensional analysis derives denoising test error and quantifies the benefit of a skip connection in a two-layer nonlinear autoencoder.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a 3D scene from images with known camera poses can involve predicting a volume of distances to surfaces. Because volumetric memory grows cubically with size, coarse-to-fine methods retain only likely surface regions for further processing. This makes the classification of surface and non-surface voxels an important part of reconstruction.

The paper argues that combining all non-surface voxels into one category creates unnecessary difficulty. Voxels inside and outside a surface have intrinsically different features, so the classifier must accommodate that gap within a single class. IOAR instead uses three categories: surface, inside, and outside. It also separates occupancy prediction from truncated signed-distance prediction to avoid interference between those branches.

This design gives the refinement process a more informative account of where voxels lie relative to a surface. The authors report that improved classification enables more precise reconstructed meshes than existing methods. Experiments on ScanNet, ICL-NUIM, and TUM-RGBD demonstrate effectiveness and generalization, supporting the value of explicitly preserving the inside–outside distinction during coarse-to-fine reconstruction.
neurips-2023-inner-outer-aware-reconstru.tldr: IOAR improves volumetric scene reconstruction by distinguishing inside, outside, and surface voxels during coarse-to-fine processing.

paragraphs: Multi-step reasoning requires a model to use intermediate conclusions as it processes additional information. This paper addresses two related difficulties for language models: carrying out those reasoning steps and retaining earlier reasoning for later use. Its proposed mechanism, Self-Notes, lets a model explicitly write down thoughts while reading its input.

The distinctive feature is when those thoughts can appear. The model may interrupt its reading at any point to reason, then continue with notes interleaved among the input text. This allows reasoning to develop alongside the incoming context. Earlier conclusions can become useful information for later steps, linking the method's reasoning and memory functions within the same process.

Experiments across a wide variety of tasks show that Self-Notes can outperform chain-of-thought and scratchpad methods. The reported result supports allowing intermediate reasoning during context processing, with those intermediate steps available for further reasoning. The claim is that this arrangement can improve performance on the tested tasks; it does not imply that taking notes is uniformly superior for every language-model task.
neurips-2023-learning-to-reason-and-memo.tldr: Self-Notes lets language models interleave thoughts with input text, helping them retain intermediate reasoning and solve multi-step tasks.

paragraphs: Combinatorial optimization involves searching among discrete candidate solutions, often under tightly structured constraints. Many such problems are NP-hard, making exact solution methods difficult to use at scale. This paper investigates whether GFlowNets can learn to generate useful candidates efficiently while accommodating the structure of different graph optimization problems.

The authors formulate different combinatorial problems as Markov decision processes and train conditional GFlowNets to sample solutions. This provides a sequential construction process for candidates rather than requiring direct search across the full solution space. They also develop training techniques for long-range credit assignment, helping connect decisions made during construction with the eventual quality of a completed solution.

The motivation includes reusing a learned policy across solution searches and generating diverse candidates. Experiments across multiple combinatorial tasks, using synthetic and realistic data, show that the resulting policies can efficiently find high-quality solutions. These findings establish practical promise for learned sequential sampling in constrained optimization. They concern solution quality and efficiency in the tested problems, without claiming that the approach produces exact optima.
neurips-2023-let-the-flows-tell-solving-.tldr: Conditional GFlowNets learn sequential solution-generation policies that efficiently find high-quality candidates for graph combinatorial optimization problems.

paragraphs: Understanding learning in recurrent neural populations requires tracking how connections change together over time. Previous work found that trained recurrent networks often have low-rank weight matrices, but that describes individual stages of learning. This paper examines the tensor formed by collecting weight matrices throughout the learning process.

The authors fit recurrent networks of different ranks to large-scale neural recordings from a motor-learning task. They find that the inferred connectivity has low tensor rank, meaning its evolution remains within a fixed low-dimensional subspace across learning. They then validate this observation in an artificial recurrent network trained to perform the same task.

Mathematical results bound both matrix and tensor ranks under gradient-descent learning dynamics. These results show how low-tensor-rank weights can arise naturally in recurrent networks trained on low-dimensional tasks. Together, the empirical and theoretical findings describe a compact structure in how connectivity evolves, extending the focus beyond the rank of a final trained network. The approach also enables reconstruction of learning-related changes in recurrent dynamics from neural recordings.
neurips-2023-low-tensor-rank-learning-of.tldr: Neural-recording fits, trained recurrent networks, and mathematical analysis reveal low-dimensional structure in connectivity changes across learning.

paragraphs: Subgraph-based graph neural networks improve structural understanding by examining pieces of a graph, but enumerating every possible subgraph can be expensive. This paper asks whether that exhaustive examination is necessary. Its analysis shows that a small subset of subgraphs can provide a comparable level of expressivity.

The authors turn the choice of that subset into a combinatorial optimization problem. MAG-GNN uses a reinforcement-learning agent to update an initial candidate set iteratively, seeking subgraphs that are especially expressive for prediction. Learning which subgraphs to consider is therefore part of the model, replacing exhaustive enumeration with a targeted search procedure.

The paper describes this replacement as reducing exponential enumeration complexity to constant complexity for its subgraph search algorithm while retaining good expressivity. Experiments across many datasets show competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods, including improvements over many subgraph GNNs. They also demonstrate reduced running time. The combined result supports selective subgraph processing as a way to preserve useful structural information while lowering the computational burden of subgraph-based learning.
neurips-2023-mag-gnn-reinforcement-learn.tldr: MAG-GNN uses reinforcement learning to select informative subgraphs, retaining strong expressivity while reducing the cost of exhaustive subgraph processing.

paragraphs: Monocular 3D detection must infer spatial information from camera imagery, but vehicle-mounted and infrastructure-mounted cameras have different installation conditions. Their pitch angles and focal lengths vary, leading existing approaches to rely on different prior knowledge. MonoUNI seeks a shared formulation for these two detection settings.

Its first component is normalized depth, an optimization target that accounts for differences in camera pitch and focal length. The second is a 3D normalized cube-depth representation for obstacles, designed to provide richer depth clues during learning. The authors argue that the amount of available depth information is important to detection performance on both sides, motivating a representation that supports better spatial understanding.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on five benchmarks without introducing extra information. The evaluations cover infrastructure-side detection with Rope3D and DAIR-V2X-I, vehicle-side detection with KITTI and Waymo, and cross-dataset evaluation with nuScenes. These results support a unified approach built around a shared depth target and richer depth supervision, rather than treating the two camera-placement settings as separate detection problems.
neurips-2023-monouni-a-unified-vehicle-a.tldr: MonoUNI unifies vehicle- and infrastructure-side monocular 3D detection through normalized depth and richer obstacle-depth representations.

paragraphs: Multilabel ranking concerns ordering labels according to their relevance. This paper studies the fundamental question of when such a ranking problem is learnable when feedback consists of relevance scores. Its focus is on the possibility of learning across a broad family of ranking losses, the criteria used to judge ranking errors.

The authors characterize learnability in both batch and online settings. Addressing both settings makes the analysis relevant to learning from a collected dataset and to learning as examples arrive over time. The central contribution is a theoretical characterization across these settings, connecting the ranking task and its evaluation loss to whether learning is possible.

The work also identifies two equivalence classes of losses based on learnability, covering most ranking losses used in practice. This groups different ways of scoring ranking mistakes according to their learnability behavior. Such a classification gives a common theoretical organization to losses that may otherwise appear separate. The stated result concerns these learnability relationships under relevance-score feedback, rather than an empirical comparison of particular ranking systems.
neurips-2023-on-the-learnability-of-mult.tldr: The paper characterizes multilabel-ranking learnability with relevance-score feedback and organizes practical ranking losses into two learnability equivalence classes.

paragraphs: Continual learning aims to incorporate new tasks or data distributions while retaining earlier capabilities. With pretrained models, useful representations are already available, but directly using them can leave distribution gaps, while adapting parameters can introduce forgetting. RanPAC explores a simple approach based on frozen random projections and accumulated class prototypes.

The method inserts a fixed random-projection layer with a nonlinear activation between pretrained features and the output head. This expands the feature dimension and captures interactions that improve linear separation for prototype-based classification. The authors also show the importance of decorrelating class prototypes to reduce distribution disparities when working with pretrained representations.

These components support both class-incremental and domain-incremental learning while bypassing forgetting associated with parameter updates. On seven class-incremental benchmarks using pretrained ViT-B/16 models, RanPAC reduces final error rates by 20% to 62% relative to previous methods, without rehearsal memory. The results demonstrate substantial value in extracting and reorganizing existing representations, showing that effective continual learning can benefit from a comparatively simple, training-free projection mechanism.
neurips-2023-ranpac-random-projections-a.tldr: RanPAC combines frozen random projections and accumulated class prototypes to improve continual learning from pretrained models without rehearsal memory.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement-learning algorithms have improved substantially, but their performance can depend on small design decisions as well as their central algorithmic ideas. This paper asks how much established, simpler methods can gain from those decisions. It revisits recent work to identify design elements worth incorporating into an existing baseline.

The resulting method, ReBRAC, builds on TD3+BC while retaining a minimalist approach. Its contribution is the integration and investigation of these design elements within that foundation. This matters for interpreting progress: improvements attributed to increasingly elaborate algorithms may also involve choices whose benefits extend to simpler methods.

The authors evaluate ReBRAC on 51 D4RL and V-D4RL datasets, covering both proprioceptive and visual state spaces. They report state-of-the-art performance among ensemble-free methods in offline and offline-to-online settings. Thousands of experiments further examine individual design choices through ablations and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis. Together, these results establish a strong minimalist method and provide extensive evidence about the importance of design decisions surrounding an algorithm's core.
neurips-2023-revisiting-the-minimalist-a.tldr: ReBRAC strengthens TD3+BC with studied design choices, achieving leading ensemble-free results across offline and offline-to-online reinforcement-learning evaluations.

paragraphs: Feature attribution assigns importance to individual inputs, while feature interactions describe contributions involving groups of inputs. Shapley interaction indices extend Shapley values to those groups. Several definitions exist because they follow different axioms, and existing definitions have required their own approximation techniques.

SHAP-IQ provides a shared sampling-based approximation method for arbitrary cardinal interaction indices satisfying linearity, symmetry, and the dummy axiom. Its new representation supports interactions of any order, allowing groups of different sizes to be considered within the same framework. The authors provide theoretical guarantees for approximation quality and estimates of the variance of the resulting point estimates.

For ordinary Shapley values, the framework yields a new representation corresponding to Unbiased KernelSHAP with a much simpler calculation. Applications to language models, image classification, and high-dimensional synthetic models illustrate computational efficiency and effectiveness. The contribution unifies estimation across a broad, explicitly defined family of interaction measures. It does not settle which interaction definition is uniquely preferable; it makes supported definitions more accessible through a common approximation procedure.
neurips-2023-shap-iq-unified-approximati.tldr: SHAP-IQ offers a unified sampling method with approximation guarantees for a broad family of Shapley interactions of any order.

paragraphs: Many structured datasets involve interactions among groups rather than only pairs. Hypergraphs represent these higher-order connections, but the representation still leaves choices about how information should move through them. This paper enriches hypergraphs with cellular sheaves, adding mathematical structure while preserving their local group connectivity.

The authors develop linear and nonlinear sheaf hypergraph Laplacians, operators that underpin information processing on the enriched structure. Their theoretical analysis shows that adding sheaves provides a more expressive inductive bias than standard hypergraph diffusion. In practical terms, the model gains a richer built-in way to represent and process relationships within higher-order data.

These operators lead to two model families: Sheaf Hypergraph Neural Networks and Sheaf Hypergraph Convolutional Networks. Both generalize classical hypergraph networks, connecting the new construction to established approaches. Extensive experiments show significant improvements and top results on multiple hypergraph node-classification benchmarks. The paper therefore links a mathematical extension of hypergraph processing to stronger predictive results in the evaluated tasks, with theory explaining the added expressive structure.
neurips-2023-sheaf-hypergraph-networks-8.tldr: Sheaf Hypergraph Networks enrich higher-order message processing with cellular sheaves, improving expressivity and benchmark node-classification performance.

paragraphs: Expressive human pose and shape estimation combines body, hand, and face motion capture in one task. This paper investigates how far the field can progress by scaling both training data and model capacity. The resulting generalist model, SMPLer-X, uses vision-transformer backbones up to ViT-Huge and as many as 4.5 million training instances.

The data study examines 32 datasets spanning scenarios that a model trained on any single dataset cannot handle. The authors use this benchmarking to select datasets and improve the training scheme. Alongside that investigation, they study how performance changes with vision-transformer size, treating data selection and model scaling as complementary parts of building broader capabilities.

SMPLer-X performs strongly across diverse test settings and transfers well to previously unseen environments. The authors report state-of-the-art results on seven benchmarks and show that additional finetuning can turn the generalist model into stronger specialists. These findings support the value of broad, carefully selected training data combined with larger models, while also demonstrating a route from general-purpose estimation to task-specific improvements.
neurips-2023-smpler-x-scaling-up-express.tldr: SMPLer-X scales diverse training data and vision transformers to improve unified body, hand, and face estimation across benchmarks and unseen environments.

paragraphs: Neural networks trained to minimize average error can rely on spurious correlations and perform poorly on minority groups. Retraining only the final layer can improve group robustness, but the DFR approach requires group and class labels for a balanced held-out dataset. This paper investigates how much of that annotation requirement can be removed.

The authors find that final-layer retraining can substantially improve worst-group accuracy even when relatively few retraining examples come from the worst-performing group. Holding out part of the original training data for this purpose can outperform training with all the data, without additional data, annotations, or training computation. Their broader low-annotation setup still uses group annotations for model selection.

The proposed SELF method selects retraining examples through misclassifications or model disagreements. Experiments provide evidence that disagreement enriches the selected set with worst-group examples. Across four vision and language benchmarks, SELF nearly matches DFR while using less than 3% of the held-out class annotations and no group annotations for constructing the retraining set. The findings make final-layer retraining more practical under limited labeling resources.
neurips-2023-towards-last-layer-retraini.tldr: Selective final-layer retraining nearly matches DFR's group robustness with far fewer labels, while still using group annotations for model selection.

paragraphs: Some problems require exploring alternatives before committing to a solution, especially when early choices determine what is possible later. This paper introduces Tree of Thoughts, an inference framework that lets language models search across intermediate reasoning steps. It extends chain-of-thought prompting by treating coherent pieces of text as units of exploration.

The model can consider several reasoning paths and evaluate its own candidate steps to decide how to proceed. It can also look ahead or backtrack when needed. This creates a process in which intermediate decisions can be compared and revisited, giving the model a way to make choices based on more than its immediate continuation.

Experiments examine Game of 24, Creative Writing, and Mini Crosswords, three tasks requiring substantial planning or search. The authors report significant improvements across these tasks. In Game of 24, GPT-4 with chain-of-thought prompting solves 4% of tasks, while Tree of Thoughts reaches 74%. The result illustrates how changing the inference procedure can substantially improve problem solving in settings where exploring alternative paths matters.
neurips-2023-tree-of-thoughts-deliberate.tldr: Tree of Thoughts improves language-model problem solving by searching, evaluating, and revisiting alternative intermediate reasoning paths.

paragraphs: This paper studies what a single multi-head attention layer can represent and learn under a controlled random-feature setup. The input consists of key vectors and a separate query. Query and key matrices are randomly sampled and frozen, while value matrices are trained, allowing the authors to analyze learning within a precisely specified architecture.

They show that the layer can express a broad class of functions whose outputs do not depend on the ordering of the key vectors. They also derive quantitative excess-risk bounds for finite training samples and finitely many heads. These results connect representational capability with the amount of data needed to learn supported functions.

The analysis identifies sample-complexity advantages over standard two-layer random-feature networks and concrete function classes that attention can learn efficiently. It also shows that nonzero-mean Gaussian query-key weights improve sample complexity over zero-mean weights for certain natural targets. Simulated experiments support the theory and illustrate interactions between sample size and target complexity. These conclusions concern the stated random-feature attention setting and its supported target functions.
neurips-2023-what-can-a-single-attention.tldr: A random-feature analysis characterizes functions a single attention layer can learn and identifies conditional sample-efficiency advantages.

paragraphs: Understanding graph neural networks on large graphs requires studying what they can predict about individual nodes. This paper develops that perspective through random-graph models, examining the functions GNNs approach as graph size grows. Its focus complements expressivity analyses centered on graph isomorphism or whole-graph prediction.

The authors give a more complete description of the function space generated by equivariant GNNs for node-level tasks. Their convergence framework encompasses several earlier results and highlights the importance of input node features. They particularly examine positional encodings, which add information about a node's position in the graph, and study how those inputs affect what the network can compute.

By analyzing several positional encodings, the paper extends previously known universality results to substantially more general random-graph models. The theory also suggests normalization choices that improve generalization numerically on synthetic and real data. New concentration inequalities support the proofs. Together, these contributions connect large-graph expressivity with input representation choices and offer theoretically motivated adjustments whose benefits are demonstrated in experiments.
neurips-2023-what-functions-can-graph-ne.tldr: The paper characterizes large-random-graph GNN expressivity and shows how positional encodings expand theoretical capabilities and motivate useful normalization choices.
